video_title: The Big Squeeze: High Bond Yields Becoming A Problem For Stocks | Jan van Eck
gist: Jan van Eck argues Q3's 10-year yield spike is growth-driven, not an inflation or credit scare, creating a 'bond squeeze' that makes ~5% bonds compete with equities, so VanEck trimmed its bond underweight while staying overweight tech/AI and real assets. Colleague Christian Munafo adds that frontier labs keep >70% of AI revenue despite open models taking >70% of tokens, and that private markets are booming but illiquid and power-law driven.

insights.claim: Jan van Eck calls Q3 2026 'the bond squeeze': the rise in the 10-year yield makes fixed income (e.g., high-yield munis yielding high single digits) competitive with ~8% annualized equity returns, pulling money from other parts of portfolios.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Higher risk-free and credit yields raise the hurdle for every other asset; expect rotation into bonds.
insights.quote: yields are getting to be relatively attractive especially you know like high yield munis and things like that are are in the high single digits that's competing with annualized equity returns of 8% % a year

insights.claim: Four of the five top-inflow funds at VanEck over the past month or so have been fixed income funds, evidence of a shift in investor portfolios toward bonds.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Flow data confirms retail/advisor rotation into fixed income at current yields.
insights.quote: the four out of the five top inflow funds have been fixed income funds

insights.claim: VanEck remains structurally underweight bonds due to US deficit concerns, but its model portfolios started buying bonds last week and slightly reduced the underweight because yields are now more attractive short term.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: A long-term bond bear is tactically adding duration at 5%+ yields - a sign yields may be near a near-term ceiling.
insights.quote: in our models um Adam we've started buying bonds

insights.claim: Van Eck argues the 10-year yield rise is driven by strong economic growth (rising nominal GDP raising credit demand and real yields), not by credit fears, inflation, or a loss of confidence in the US.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Growth-driven yield rises are less dangerous than inflation- or credit-driven ones; don't read it as a crisis signal.
insights.quote: the rise in interest rates is not due to credit concerns. Um, it's not due to inflation concerns, but it's due to economic growth

insights.claim: The oil-bonds correlation narrative tied to the Iran conflict/Strait of Hormuz is called 'fake news': yields didn't rise for many months of the war and higher oil, the correlation held only weeks in late summer, and recently oil rose while yields fell.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Don't trade bonds off oil headlines; the link was temporary, not fundamental.
insights.quote: that's sort of a little bit of a fake news narrative

insights.claim: Rising real yields (yields less inflation) indicate a booming economy and credit demand rather than inflation, since inflation-driven moves would leave real yields flat.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Watch real yields to diagnose whether rate rises are growth- or inflation-driven.

insights.claim: Van Eck says ~2% real yields are not abnormal once the post-financial-crisis period of unprecedented policy is excluded from comparisons; some VanEck colleagues think real yields are not high enough.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: 'Highest in 20 years' framing is misleading; real yields could stay or go higher without being extreme.
insights.quote: you really have to throw out this entire post financial crisis time period

insights.claim: The strongest reason Van Eck is not worried about the bond selloff is that the US dollar has held strong against other developed-market currencies; a genuine 'sell America' move would hit the dollar too.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Use dollar strength as a check on 'foreigners fleeing US assets' narratives.
insights.quote: if people were really selling the United States, they'd be selling the US dollar as well

insights.claim: Higher yields have already hurt rate-sensitive areas such as the equal-weight S&P, the Dow, homebuilders, and housing via mortgage rates; Van Eck also cites a number of failed IPOs in Asia and the US over the prior two weeks.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Much of the rate pain may already be priced in rate-sensitive sectors.

insights.claim: Van Eck and David Hay (cited from the conference) are 'renting the rally' in bonds: duration is hard to get right, there is little technical support for yields at 5.25-6%, fixed income buyers emerge around 5.5% and riskier buyers want 6%+, and 2-year paper paying ~5% offers attractive yield with little duration risk.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Favor short duration (~2-year) to collect ~5%; treat any long-bond rally as tradable, not structural.
insights.quote: if you look at 2-year duration, wow, that's pretty attractive, right? You're not taking a lot of duration risk and you're getting paid 5%

themes.theme: Fiscal deficit and global bond demand

insights.claim: Van Eck views fiscal policy as still stimulative ('one foot on the gas pedal') and expects no change after the midterms because divided parties are unlikely to agree to contract spending.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Continued fiscal stimulus supports near-term growth but sustains deficit pressure on bonds.

insights.claim: Van Eck sees monetary policy as roughly neutral rather than stimulative, noting the Fed raised rates, though there is considerable internal disagreement at VanEck on that view.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Don't count on Fed easing as a tailwind for risk assets.
insights.quote: the Fed raised rates

insights.claim: The US fiscal deficit worsened instead of improving, hitting about $2 trillion, as tax revenue fell short (mostly lost tariff revenue) while outlays kept rising; Van Eck calls it an untimeable long-term problem (5 or 10 years).
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Structural reason to stay underweight long bonds and overweight real assets, despite inability to time it.
insights.quote: the budget deficit hit two trillion

insights.claim: With higher global rates, Japanese investors now get better yields buying JGBs at home than currency-hedged US Treasuries, reducing marginal foreign demand for Treasuries - not a loss of faith in the US but 'grocery economics'.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Treasuries now compete for global capital; foreign demand is price-sensitive, which supports higher US yields.
insights.quote: it's just grocery economics, right? I buy the cheaper bananas

insights.claim: Citing Fred Hickey's newsletter, Van Eck notes China (non-central-bank/private buyers) is purchasing about 46% of global gold production this year, double last year's pace and an all-time record, while China's Treasury holdings are about half their 2013 peak.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Chinese private gold demand is a structural bid; China is a shrinking Treasury buyer.

themes.theme: AI megatrend: demand modeling and public-market discipline

insights.claim: Van Eck argues that being out of or underweight tech/AI has been very expensive year to date and since the ChatGPT moment; VanEck is overweight tech above an already tech-dominant S&P 500 and overweights semis in its models.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Underweighting the AI trade carries large opportunity cost; bears must be right to justify it.
insights.quote: if you listen to the naysayers or stepped out of this mega tent trend trade of tech, you are leaving a lot of money on the table

insights.claim: Megacap tech earnings expectations show a slight slowdown in year-over-year growth, and Van Eck strips out one-time gains from marking up private stakes such as Anthropic and SpaceX that have been inflating reported quarterly earnings.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Adjust big-tech EPS for private-stake markups to judge true earnings quality.

insights.claim: VanEck analyst Angus Shillington modeled AI demand from token usage: individual VanEck employees' token use rises ~8x from month two to month twelve of adoption, then ~25% a year; extrapolated to the market it matched the industry projection of ~5x demand growth, while holding training compute flat as a conservative assumption.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: AI demand is becoming modelable like other sectors; inference (not training) is the projected growth driver, with upside if training grows.
insights.quote: your token usage goes up like eight times and then after that it goes up at sort of like 25% a year

insights.claim: The AI trade is transitioning from a purely supply-constrained phase (TSMC, memory output) to one where demand-side token data can drive earnings projections, though supply shortages persist.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Analysts should shift toward demand-based models for AI earnings.

insights.claim: Semiconductors are up ~50% year to date while Nvidia is up only ~16% and its valuation has come down dramatically, making it more attractive.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Nvidia has de-rated relative to the semi complex, improving its risk/reward.

insights.claim: Van Eck calls Nvidia the 'IBM' of the AI hardware ecosystem - generating cash, buying back shares, paying dividends and extending guidance a year out - and says it is a fundamentally different company from prior gaming/Bitcoin-mining cycles.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Nvidia's capital return and guidance signal durability rather than cyclical peak.
insights.quote: now they are the like I call them the IBM of that system

insights.claim: Van Eck sent clients a cautionary note on memory chip companies in Q2 and won't overvalue them, describing them as still 'teenagers' versus mature Nvidia; he notes he correctly called Nvidia overdone at 50x sales in summer 2024.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Within semis, be wary of cyclical memory names despite the AI boom.

insights.claim: The 'AI needs old-world power and data centers' trade corrected this year because names like utilities and independent power producer Vistra had traded above fair valuations; Vistra's long-term contracted power now trades at more attractive valuations.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: AI-power beneficiaries like Vistra may now offer better entry points.

insights.claim: CoreWeave's recent drop reflects price discipline on compute providers with weaker financials, likely amplified by higher rates; Van Eck notes CoreWeave and Oracle both fell ~50% in Q4 2025 as well, so it is a recurring pattern, not a trend break.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Leveraged AI infrastructure names are most exposed to the bond squeeze; selloffs there don't negate the megatrend.

insights.claim: AI has crushed software and adjacent consulting stocks like Accenture, but Van Eck says AI isn't eliminating those jobs wholesale; AI has three components - data, software and people - and companies (including VanEck) are pivoting spending toward clean data.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Data infrastructure is an emerging AI 2.0 beneficiary; software/consulting selloff may be overdone.
insights.quote: AI has three components data software and people

insights.claim: Van Eck says Q1 2026's breakthrough was corporate America becoming the end consumer of AI via Anthropic, which underpins the quality of AI earnings; Christian Munafo adds most AI revenue comes from large, well-capitalized established firms rather than thinly capitalized startups.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Enterprise demand reduces circular-financing/earnings-quality risk concerns.

insights.claim: Van Eck sees nothing systemic in Q3 that ends the AI trend, and says the public markets show more discipline than private markets, where it's 'both feet on the gas'.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Stay invested in public AI; be more cautious with private AI valuations.
insights.quote: there's nothing so systemic that happened in Q3 that would lead me to say this thing this trend is over

themes.theme: Frontier vs open models and desktop real estate

insights.claim: Open-source models now account for over 70% of token consumption, yet Anthropic and OpenAI still capture over 70% of revenue share, because high-value enterprise use cases (coding, forecasting, agentic workflows) pay a premium for frontier capability and security.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: Usage share is a misleading metric; value capture remains with frontier labs.

insights.claim: Open-weight models lag frontier models by roughly four to six months, a gap that has stayed fairly consistent per Epoch AI tracking, as frontier labs keep improving and likely withhold their most powerful models.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: The frontier moat is persistent rather than eroding, supporting frontier pricing power.

insights.claim: Anthropic reportedly put up about $16-17 billion in revenue last quarter, only a few years after starting to generate revenue.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab revenue scale is enormous; relevant for any Anthropic IPO.
insights.quote: they put up 16 billion, almost 17 billion in revenue

insights.claim: Munafo expects frontier model pricing to fall over time, AWS-style, with broader adoption offsetting lower prices; adoption is still in early innings.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: Expect price deflation per token but volume-driven growth.

insights.claim: Van Eck frames the AI battle as one for 'corporate desktop real estate': whichever tool (e.g., Claude, even as interface to the Microsoft suite) gets connected to company databases gains sticky positioning due to switching and retraining costs.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Enterprise switching costs create durable moats for the incumbent AI interface.
insights.quote: it's all about location, location, location

insights.claim: Soaring valuations of private inference-cloud companies are a 'tell' that confirms the projected surge in inference demand, though Munafo cautions such private-market signals sometimes blow up.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: Private valuations can be a leading indicator for public AI sub-sectors.

insights.claim: Munafo argues next-generation technologies (photonics, quantum, more efficient interconnects and switching, lower power consumption) will make AI infrastructure far more efficient and better utilize under-used capacity.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: Efficiency tech may temper the old-world power/buildout trade and is a private-market opportunity.

themes.theme: Private markets: scale, illiquidity, and power law

insights.claim: The number of US listed companies has roughly halved over recent decades while private companies have soared to 50-60,000, with about $11 trillion in total US venture company value.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: An increasing share of economic growth sits outside listed markets.

insights.claim: Venture-backed tech companies once IPO'd ~4 years from inception at ~$0.5B market cap; now they stay private 12-15 years (SpaceX 24 years) and list at multiples higher, e.g., SpaceX at over a trillion.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: Public investors miss much of the growth phase; private access has rising value.

insights.claim: The private market has a 'TVPI glut': paper value (total value to paid-in) far exceeds realized distributions (DPI is historically low) because COVID, 2022-24 rate hikes and a still-closed IPO window have limited exits, with exit value concentrated in a few names like SpaceX.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: Judge private funds on DPI, not marked-up value; liquidity is scarce.
insights.quote: the IPO window in our view is far from open

insights.claim: Roughly 90% of venture returns over recent decades came from 5% of managers, and fewer than 1% of ~3,000 VC managers consistently returned more than 3x; first-time managers struggle to raise capital as LPs favor incumbents.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: Manager selection dominates private-market outcomes.

insights.claim: Munafo says private AI is 'unshakingly booming' with valuations hard to justify - one unnamed AI company was valued near $25 billion before releasing a model, and hard-tech firms with only prototypes get scale-manufacturing valuations; many assets are priced to perfection.
insights.speaker: Christian Munafo
insights.so_what: Private AI shows bubble-like pricing; discipline and caution warranted.
insights.quote: They were valued at close to $25 billion and they had not yet released their model

themes.theme: Private credit, real assets, energy, gold

insights.claim: Van Eck admits his Q2 call to buy private credit manager equities failed: Blue Owl rallied ~30% from ~$9 to over $12 but gave it all back, squeezed by higher bond yields and elevated redemption requests at a major fund; he is holding his personal position.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Private credit vehicles' 9-10% yields lose appeal when the 10-year pays over 5%.
insights.quote: it's one thing to offer 9% 10% yields in a zero interest rate environment it's different if the um you know if the 10-year bond is offering uh o over 5%

insights.claim: Van Eck says private credit pressure is mainly rate-driven, not imploding holdings; first-half headwinds were under-reported regulatory scrutiny over mismarking and software/SaaS pressure, which he sees as priced in, and he doesn't predict lower lows, while Blue Owl's dividend pays you to wait.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Contagion fears look overstated; rate path is the key driver.

insights.claim: The share of leveraged loans marked below ~80 cents on the dollar rose in the first half of 2026 and has plateaued, while high-yield issuance has slowed; private credit stress emerges with a lag, possibly taking years to work through like commercial real estate.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: A metric to monitor for lagged credit stress from higher rates.

insights.claim: Gold miners have paid down the large net debt they carried in the zero-rate era, and energy companies likewise are no longer leveraged players.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Commodity producers are fundamentally stronger than in past cycles.

insights.claim: Resource companies are finding little new gold or oil and exploration spending remains disciplined, so existing reserves held by incumbents are increasingly valuable.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Scarcity supports incumbent producer valuations.

insights.claim: US shale growth of 8-10 million barrels a day is unlikely to repeat while global oil demand keeps rising, and energy equities aren't pricing in the still-high 2027 oil futures.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Energy stocks embed a discount vs the commodity curve - potential upside.

insights.claim: Energy companies' 2-4% dividends look dull in a 5% rate world, but including buybacks their shareholder yield is in the high single to low double digits for some VanEck holdings - investors looking only at dividends miss two-thirds of the story.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Screen energy on shareholder yield, not dividend yield.
insights.quote: You're you're missing actually twothirds of the story

insights.claim: Financial advisors are way underweight real assets versus 10-20 years ago, partly passively as tech grew and energy's S&P weight shrank; VanEck stays structurally overweight real assets to smooth returns and hedge eventual US spending risk.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Real assets are under-owned, a contrarian diversification opportunity.

insights.claim: Van Eck remains 10-year very bullish on gold, sees early innings of a long bull market, accepts a 1-2 year correction after the run to all-time highs, and notes the correction has held $4,000 an ounce; higher global real rates weigh on non-yielding gold.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Use corrections above $4,000 to build long-term gold exposure.
insights.quote: It it's held $4,000 an ounce

insights.claim: Van Eck calls India his worst call: it was hurt by the Iran conflict as an energy importer, tariffs, and AI disruption of its IT outsourcing without upside from native memory chip makers.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: India is an AI loser and oil-shock loser near term.

insights.claim: After broad capitulation, Indian equities are reaching the bottom of their historically expensive valuation range, making it one of the cheaper entry points in four years; Van Eck suggests dollar-cost averaging for adventurous investors, citing equity culture, hundreds of IPOs a year, deregulation and digitization, and a consumer market projected to match Europe in 10 years.
insights.speaker: Jan van Eck
insights.so_what: Contrarian entry point for a 10-year India thesis.
insights.quote: now that everyone, you know, has given up on India, it's finally getting to the bottom of its valuation range
